title: Porphyria cutanea tarda (& pseudoporphyria)
summary: Fragile skin, blisters, erosions, scars and milia on the backs of the hands, with facial hair growth and dark urine. Look for alcohol, hepatitis C, haemochromatosis, oestrogens and HIV; pseudoporphyria from drugs looks the same.

glance.think: Blisters and erosions on the backs of the hands after minor knocks, healing with scars and milia; facial hypertrichosis; reddish-brown urine.
glance.engine: Reduced hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity (iron, alcohol, hepatitis C, oestrogen) causes porphyrin build-up that reacts with visible light.
glance.backbone: Refer for porphyrin testing; stop alcohol and oestrogens; screen liver, iron, hepatitis B/C and HIV; specialist venesection or low-dose hydroxychloroquine; visible-light protection.
glance.never_miss: Underlying liver disease or hepatocellular carcinoma; haemochromatosis; pseudoporphyria from naproxen or other drugs.

what: The commonest porphyria worldwide: a **blistering photosensitivity with skin fragility** caused by reduced activity of the hepatic haem-pathway enzyme **uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD)**. Usually presents in middle-aged adults (more often men). **Sporadic/acquired (type 1, ~75–80%)** or **familial (type 2, inherited heterozygous UROD mutation)** — the latter still needs acquired triggers to become clinically active. A **non-acute** porphyria: no neurovisceral attacks.
cause: When hepatic UROD activity falls below ~20–25% of normal, **uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrins accumulate in the liver**, spill into plasma and urine, and deposit in skin. Porphyrins absorb strongly in the **Soret band (~400–410 nm, visible violet light)**, generating reactive oxygen species → damage at the dermo-epidermal junction → fragility and subepidermal blisters. **Triggers / associations (mostly hepatic iron and oxidative stress):**

list: **Alcohol** (Case 2: ~40 units/week) and **smoking** (Case 2: 10/day)
**Iron overload** — including **HFE haemochromatosis** mutations
**Hepatitis C** (also hepatitis B), **HIV**
**Oestrogens** (COC, HRT, prostate cancer therapy)
Chronic kidney disease/haemodialysis; occasionally hepatocellular carcinoma ("hepatic porphyrinoma"); polyhalogenated aromatic hydrocarbons (historical)

cause: **Liver** is the internal organ most affected: steatosis, siderosis, fibrosis/cirrhosis and raised risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

list: **Tense vesicles and bullae (some haemorrhagic)** on **dorsal hands and fingers**, forearms, face, and scalp/ears in bald men — often after minor knocks.
**Skin fragility**: erosions and crusts from trivial trauma; slow healing over weeks.
**Milia**, atrophic and white/pink scars on dorsal hands.
**Hypertrichosis** of temples/cheeks, mottled hyper/hypopigmentation, sclerodermoid thickening (late).
**Dark, red-brown or "tea"/port-wine urine**; fluoresces pink-red under Wood's lamp.
Worse in summer (Case 2) — but patients often don't link it to sun, because the trigger is visible light through windows and damage is delayed.

**Most relevant first test: urine (and/or plasma) porphyrins** — raised uroporphyrin and heptacarboxylic porphyrin; faecal isocoproporphyrin raised. Plasma fluorescence emission peak ~619–620 nm distinguishes PCT from variegate porphyria (~626 nm) — this matters because variegate porphyria can cause acute attacks. ALA and porphobilinogen normal.

**Associated-cause work-up:** LFTs, **ferritin + transferrin saturation**, **HFE genotyping**, **hepatitis C and B, HIV serology**, glucose/HbA1c, renal function, consider liver ultrasound (± HCC surveillance if cirrhotic), ANA if diagnostic overlap.
Skin biopsy (subepidermal blister with "festooning" of dermal papillae; immunofluorescence) when needed to exclude other bullous disease.
Sent via specialist porphyria laboratory; UK National Acute Porphyria Service / specialist dermatology.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Same clinical picture but **normal porphyrins**; drugs — **naproxen** (and other NSAIDs), tetracyclines, **furosemide**, bumetanide, nalidixic acid, isotretinoin, dapsone, voriconazole; **sunbeds**; haemodialysis. Hypertrichosis and dark urine absent. Stop the drug/sunbed.
Same skin changes **plus risk of acute neurovisceral attacks** — porphyrin pattern differs; dangerous drug list applies
Trauma-induced blisters/milia, but not photo-related; biopsy/immunofluorescence
Elderly, itchy urticated plaques + tense blisters trunk/flexures
Bullous drug eruption / fixed drug eruption
Acute single episode; streaks; no fragility/milia
Childhood, immediate burning pain in sun, little blistering

differentials.title: Full PCT coverage
differentials.text: (pathophysiology, urine porphyrin testing, venesection, low-dose hydroxychloroquine, visible-light sunscreen) is in the [photodermatoses](condition:polymorphic-light-eruption) notes. Only the case-specific points and the mimics are covered here.

differentials: PCT is the **commonest porphyria**. It comes from reduced **hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD)** activity, which is acquired (type 1, ~80%) or familial (type 2). Uroporphyrins build up and cause **blistering photosensitivity on sun-exposed skin**.

Porphyrins absorb visible light (Soret band ~400–410 nm), which damages the dermal–epidermal junction, so the skin becomes fragile and blisters below the epidermis. **Triggers that the history in Case 3 points to:**

list: **alcohol** (dependence)
**hepatitis C** and **HIV** (homelessness and possible injecting drug use, which may also explain the **forearm scars**)
**iron overload / HFE haemochromatosis**
oestrogens
smoking

**fragile skin, tense and haemorrhagic blisters and erosions on the backs of the hands** after minor trauma (Case 3; photo D01, and the [photodermatoses](condition:polymorphic-light-eruption) notes B01–B06)
healing with **scarring, milia** and dyspigmentation
**facial hypertrichosis** (upper cheeks and temples)
photo-distributed hyperpigmentation or "tanned" face
morphoea-like sclerodermoid plaques later on
**dark or red-brown urine**

differentials: Urine porphyrins (a random urine sample **protected from light**; it may glow pink under Wood's lamp), plasma porphyrins with a **plasma fluorescence emission scan (peak ~619 nm)** to separate PCT from variegate porphyria, and stool porphyrins. Add LFT, **ferritin/transferrin saturation, HFE genotype**, **HCV, HBV and HIV serology**, glucose and liver ultrasound (HCC risk). Skin biopsy with DIF (perivascular IgG/C3) is not usually needed. Specialist support: **UK Porphyria Medicines Information Service / National Acute Porphyria Service**, Cardiff and King's.

list: **Pseudoporphyria**: looks the same but porphyrins are **normal**. Drug causes are **naproxen** and other NSAIDs, tetracyclines, nalidixic acid, furosemide, retinoids, and **sunbeds**. Also seen in dialysis. Stop the drug (**Module 5 exam Q2**).

**Variegate porphyria / hereditary coproporphyria:** the skin looks the same, but there is a risk of **acute neurovisceral attacks** with porphyrinogenic drugs. This is why the plasma scan matters before choosing drugs.
**EBA**: trauma-induced acral blisters, scarring and milia; porphyrins normal; linear IgG on the *dermal* floor of salt-split skin.

**BP**, **bullous impetigo**, **friction or trauma blisters** (rough sleeping), **bullous drug eruption**, **bullosis diabeticorum**, **burns** (cigarettes in intoxication), and **erythropoietic protoporphyria** (painful, burning, no blisters, children).

Refer to dermatology or hepatology (routine to urgent). Treat the drivers: **alcohol cessation** (local alcohol services, thiamine), **HCV direct-acting antivirals** (which often cure PCT), and stop oestrogens. Specialists then use **venesection** (to ferritin ~20 µg/L) or **low-dose hydroxychloroquine 100–200 mg twice weekly** (*not* daily, which causes hepatotoxicity), with eye screening per the RCOphth schedule. **Visible-light protection:** reflectant tinted sunscreen such as zinc/titanium with iron oxides; standard UV sunscreen is not enough.

**Social context for Case 3:** homelessness makes venesection and follow-up hard. Arrange a GP registration route, link with the hepatology outreach or HCV peer-support team, and give **gloves and hand protection**.
**Blisters on the backs of the hands plus hypertrichosis or dark urine: check porphyrins and do a medication review (NSAIDs, so think pseudoporphyria).**
The porphyria drug-safety database (Welsh Medicines Information / NAPS) matters for **acute** porphyrias, *not* for PCT. Until the plasma scan excludes variegate porphyria, prescribe cautiously.

See the the [photodermatoses](condition:polymorphic-light-eruption) notes URL list. DermNet: [dermnetnz.org](https://dermnetnz.org/topics/pseudoporphyria) · [dermnetnz.org](https://dermnetnz.org/topics/epidermolysis-bullosa-acquisita)
UK Porphyria Medicines Information Service / NAPS: [wmic.wales.nhs.uk](https://www.wmic.wales.nhs.uk/specialist-services/drugs-in-porphyria/)

management: **Refer** — PCT diagnosis and treatment are specialist (dermatology ± hepatology/porphyria service). The pharmacist/IP role:

list: **Recognise** the pattern (blisters + fragility + scars/milia on dorsal hands; alcohol/smoking/oestrogen/hep C) and **refer** with suspicion stated; topical steroids don't help (Case 2).

**Remove triggers:** stop alcohol and smoking (offer NHS stop-smoking support and alcohol brief intervention), **review oestrogens** (COC/HRT — discuss alternatives with prescriber), **stop iron supplements and iron-containing multivitamins**.

Specialist treatments (know, don't initiate): **venesection** (reduce ferritin), **low-dose hydroxychloroquine** (e.g. 100 mg–200 mg **twice weekly**, not standard daily antimalarial doses, which can cause hepatotoxicity), treatment of hepatitis C with direct-acting antivirals often induces remission. Chloroquine sometimes used at low dose.

**Visible-light photoprotection**: conventional chemical UV filters don't cover 400–410 nm — recommend **reflectant sunscreens containing titanium dioxide/zinc oxide, ideally tinted (iron-oxide)**, e.g. Dundee cream (via specialists) or tinted mineral SPF 50; gloves, long sleeves, hats; **window film** for car/home.
Wound care for erosions (non-adherent dressings, watch for infection); protect hands from trauma (gloves for DIY/gardening).

management: All suspected PCT → routine-soon dermatology with urine porphyrins requested in primary care if local pathway allows. Urgent if abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric features or hyponatraemia (possible acute porphyria — check drug safety via the Welsh Medicines Advice/UK Porphyria Medicines Information Service database). Signs of decompensated liver disease → urgent.
red_flags: Signs of chronic liver disease or a known liver mass: urgent review.
Ordinary sunscreens do not block visible light: use opaque or tinted (iron oxide) protection.
Do not use standard-dose hydroxychloroquine: only low-dose under specialist advice (risk of hepatotoxicity).
pearls: **Blisters on the back of the hands in a drinker = check porphyrins**; "worse in summer" but light through glass counts.
**Pseudoporphyria** is the pharmacist's catch: look for **naproxen**, doxycycline, furosemide or sunbed use — normal porphyrins, resolves (slowly, months) after withdrawal.

Before supplying drugs to anyone with a porphyria diagnosis, check porphyria drug safety lists (BNF "Acute porphyrias" section and UK Porphyria Medicines Information Service) — strictly relevant to acute porphyrias, but confirm the type.
Long-term: alcohol abstinence reduces relapse; screen for HCC if cirrhosis.
